composition.story: A language model writes one token at a time. Each new token must attend to every earlier token's keys and values. Compare two runs on "The cat sat on the mat". Without a cache, earlier keys and values are recomputed every step. With a KV cache, they are stored and reused, so only the new token is projected.

aha.observation: With a KV cache, each new token adds one key/value projection and reuses the rest. Six tokens cost 6 projections instead of 18.

controls.label: Step
controls.presentation: Previous and Next buttons with the step rail; names kept when disabled at the first and last step

controls.label: Inference mode
controls.presentation: Two-option selector that switches the run shown; step position is kept so the same step can be compared

controls.label: Reset
controls.presentation: Returns to step 1 with No cache selected

states.label: Prefill
states.sentence: Prefill: all 3 prompt tokens are projected to keys and values. Both modes do identical work here.
states.why: Starting point is the same for both runs.

states.label: Token 4
states.sentence: Token 4 arrives. With no cache, keys and values for all 4 tokens are projected again.
states.why: Tokens 1 to 3 are recomputed even though nothing about them changed.

states.label: Token 5
states.sentence: Token 5 arrives. All 5 tokens are projected again, so the repeated work grows each step.
states.why: Per-step cost rises with context length.

states.label: Token 6
states.sentence: Token 6 arrives. All 6 tokens are projected again, though only one is new.
states.why: Five of the six projections repeat earlier results.

states.label: Total cost
states.sentence: Total without a cache: 18 key/value projections for 6 tokens. Switch to KV cache to compare.
states.why: This is the baseline total the cache will cut.

regions.label: KV cache (stored rows)
values: one K/V row per token, kept

regions.label: Attention
values: newest query over all cached rows

states.label: Prefill
states.sentence: Prefill: all 3 prompt tokens are projected to keys and values and stored in the cache.
states.why: Same work as without a cache, but results are now kept.

states.label: Token 4
states.sentence: Token 4 arrives. Only its key and value are projected; the 3 cached rows are reused.
states.why: Earlier tokens are read from the cache, not recomputed.

states.label: Token 5
states.sentence: Token 5 arrives. One new key/value row is added and the 4 cached rows are reused.
states.why: Per-step projection cost stays constant at one.

states.label: Token 6
states.sentence: Token 6 arrives. One new row is added; 5 cached rows are reused, so the step stays cheap.
states.why: Context grew, but projection work did not.

states.label: Total cost
states.sentence: Total with a cache: 6 projections instead of 18. Attention still reads all 6 rows, and the cache uses memory.
states.why: The saving is in projection work; the cost is stored memory.

1.reason: The fixed picture of tokens, K/V (or cache), query and attention with active highlights answers one question: how many projections are needed with versus without a cache.

2.reason: The scene is step-driven and ends on s5, which states the 18-versus-6 totals and holds until the learner changes step or mode.

3.reason: Switching the Inference mode changes the active regions, links and readouts (new 4/5/6 versus 1, reuse 0 versus 3/4/5), and the step control moves through the states.

4.reason: Each part binds to declared data: the callout targets region kv with the state sentence, readouts come from state.readouts, the ghost uses previous.regions and the rail uses variant.states.

6.reason: The story, state sentences, region labels and the mode and step controls all use the same objects (tokens, K/V rows, cache, query), and the narrative matches the changing active sets.

7.reason: The detailed depth carries five readouts, links, a ghost, a callout and a progress trace at once, which is dense for a standard comparison, and the running-sum readout partly repeats the cumulative one.

8.reason: Every cumulative figure and running sum checks out (3, 7, 12, 18 versus 3, 4, 5, 6), but the totals 18 and 6 appear in both the sentence and the readouts, so the values are not placed only once.
